title: Orbital Compartment Syndrome: The Surgical Emergency
summary: Orbital Compartment Syndrome (OCS) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency characterized by increased intraorbital pressure leading to vascular compromise. Immediate recognition and decompression are the only definitive treatments to prevent irreversible optic nerve ischemia.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: OCS occurs when intraorbital pressure exceeds ocular perfusion pressure, leading to ischemia of the optic nerve and retina. The orbit is a closed fibro-osseous compartment; any increase in volume (hematoma, edema, emphysema) results in an exponential rise in orbital pressure (IOP + orbital venous pressure), culminating in venous stasis and rapid infarction.

content.explanation: P: Proptosis, R: Resistance to retropulsion, E: Elevated IOP (>40mmHg), S: Sight loss (APD/Decreased VA), S: Stretched/Tense lids.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis
content: Step 1: Instill proparacaine and prepare sterile field.
Step 2: Clamp lateral canthus with hemostat for 30s to crush tissue (hemostasis).
Step 3: Cut lateral canthal tendon using Stevens scissors.
Step 4: Perform superior and inferior crural cantholysis—the 'snap' confirms release.
Step 5: Re-assess IOP and visual status immediately.

rows: Fever, elevated WBC, pain on motility
Rapid onset but usually responds to steroids

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Goldmann Applanation Tonometer: IOP > 40mmHg is highly suspicious.
Urgent CT Orbit/Brain: Only if it does not delay immediate decompression.
Pupil Exam: Critical indicator of optic nerve compromise.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Do not wait for CT imaging if clinical signs are definitive.
The lateral canthal tendon consists of superior and inferior crura; both must be severed.
OCS is a 'clinical diagnosis'—eyes do not wait for imaging studies.
If IOP remains elevated post-cantholysis, consider medical adjuncts (IV Mannitol 1g/kg or Acetazolamide).

sections.title: Recent Landmark Considerations
sections.content: Recent literature emphasizes that the 'time-to-decompression' is the single most important predictor of visual recovery. Studies show that optic nerve ischemia occurs within 60-100 minutes of sustained orbital pressure elevation, suggesting that bedside lateral cantholysis is superior to any medical therapy or imaging-based delay.
